top_level_objectives: Understand the central premise of VSEPR theory: electron domains repel each other to minimize mutual repulsion.
Identify and construct the five fundamental electron-domain geometries in 3D space.
Differentiate between electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry.
Explain how lone pairs affect molecular geometry and compress ideal bond angles in real molecules.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the basic concept that electron domains (bonds and lone pairs) around a central atom repel each other to maximize distance and minimize repulsion.
key_visuals: Balloon-like electron domains that can be added one by one
A dynamic AR protractor displaying real-time bond angles
student_actions: Add two bonding domains to the central atom and observe them snap to a linear 180-degree arrangement.
Add a third domain and watch the bonds dynamically shift to a 120-degree trigonal planar arrangement.

scenes.brief_purpose: Explore the five basic electron-domain geometries formed when only bonding pairs are present around the central atom.
key_visuals: Interactive 3D models of linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral geometries
Floating holographic text labels for geometry names and ideal bond angles
student_actions: Sequentially add up to six electron domains to a central atom.
Rotate the central atom with hand gestures to observe the 3D symmetry of the tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral shapes.
Match the correct geometry name to each shape from a floating menu.

scenes.scene_name: The Tetrahedral Family and Bond Angle Deviations
scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate the effect of lone pairs on molecular geometry and bond angles using methane, ammonia, and water as primary examples.
key_visuals: 2D Lewis structures of CH4, NH3, and H2O floating in the background
3D molecular models of Methane, Ammonia, and Water
Voluminous, translucent 'clouds' representing lone pairs that visibly occupy more angular space than bonding pairs
student_actions: Convert a bonding pair in tetrahedral methane to a lone pair to form ammonia, observing the molecular geometry change to trigonal pyramidal.
Observe the bond angle compress from 109.5° to 107° due to lone pair repulsion.
Convert another bonding pair to a lone pair to form water (bent geometry) and observe the angle further compress to 104.5°.

scenes.brief_purpose: Examine how lone pairs position themselves in a trigonal bipyramidal electron-domain geometry to minimize 90-degree repulsions.
key_visuals: Color-coded visual indicators distinguishing axial from equatorial positions
Holographic lone pairs ready to be swapped with bonds
student_actions: Replace an equatorial bonding pair with a lone pair and observe the resulting 'seesaw' molecular geometry.
Attempt to place a lone pair in an axial position and watch the simulation visually reject it due to higher repulsive forces.
Add a second equatorial lone pair to form a T-shaped molecule.

scenes.brief_purpose: Explore octahedral geometries and the strategic placement of lone pairs opposite each other to minimize repulsion.
key_visuals: 3D models of SF6 (Sulfur hexafluoride) and XeF4 (Xenon tetrafluoride)
Symmetrical octahedral axes with snapping points for lone pairs
student_actions: Start with a fully bonded octahedral SF6 molecule.
Replace one bond with a lone pair to create a square pyramidal shape.
Replace a second bond with a lone pair, deliberately placing it 180 degrees away from the first to minimize repulsion, forming the square planar XeF4.

scenes.brief_purpose: Test the student's ability to apply VSEPR rules to predict 3D geometries from 2D Lewis structures.
key_visuals: A virtual whiteboard displaying a random assortment of complex Lewis structures
An empty central atom workstation with an inventory of bonding pairs and lone pairs
A dual-dropdown menu for selecting Electron Domain Geometry and Molecular Geometry
student_actions: Select a Lewis structure from the whiteboard.
Drag and drop the correct number of bonding pairs and lone pairs onto the central atom.
Predict the final electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry by selecting from the menus.
Submit the prediction and watch the constructed molecule dynamically settle into its final 3D shape to verify the answer.
